newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu leads in Romania surveys but win uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu leads in Romania surveys but win uncertain.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu, in power since the fall of Communism seven years ago, leads opinion polls before Romania's general election next week but his victory is by no means certain.

Only two of Iliescu's 15 challengers stand any chance of unseating him in next Sunday's presidential vote, the third since dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was overthrown and executed in the 1989 revolution.

But a bruising campaign, peppered with bitter accusations and allegations of dirty tricks, has not all gone Iliescu's way in the only eastern European country where former communists have yet to be thrown out of office.
The president told Reuters at a weekend campaign stop in Topoloveni, 100 km (60 miles) west of Bucharest, that he was confident of victory.

"I have this feeling, the general feeling of the people. In spite of the difficulties our society is passing through there is confidence that Romania chose the right route during the revolution," he said.
A weekend opinion poll gave Iliescu 36.5 percent support, well short of the 50 percent needed for first-round victory.

Academic Emil Constantinescu of the Democratic Convention bloc (CDR), made up of 15 parties, was second with 24.7 percent. Petre Roman, Romania's first post-Communist prime minister, stood in third with 21.7 percent.
Many voters apparently crave change. They are distressed over plunging living standards with average monthly pay below $100, far lower than in Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
Newspapers reported that Iliescu was ushered out of the back door of a theatre in Craiova, a southwestern town hard hit by economic decline, to avoid crowds of jeering students.

Even in Topoloveni, the rural bedrock of his support, the president was given no more than a polite welcome at a stage-managed rally including folk dancing and an outdoor civil wedding ceremony for a surprised young couple.
"He had good ideas at the beginning, but they haven't been carried out," said Niculina Caimac, an office worker. "I can't live on my wage (equivalent to $60). Our life is very hard."
In opinion polls for parliamentary elections also being held on Sunday, Iliescu's Party for Social Democracy (PDSR) trails the CDR and some forecasts even put it in third place.
The CDR outscored the ruling party in local elections last June, capturing most major cities.

Iliescu's rivals say he is an anachronism from a Communist system which was never really revamped. They say his reluctance to adopt fast-track reforms, like those in Poland, has plunged millions of Romanians into poverty.
News reports say Constantinescu and Roman have both drawn enthusiastic crowds in provincial towns.
"We will win this election," Constantinescu told a rally last week. "It is ours to win through historical legitimacy."

The CDR has drawn up a "contract" with voters modelled on the U.S. Republican Party and pledged to resign if it fails to implement liberal reforms within a strict time frame. Its activists dog Iliescu's rallies with posters showing a loaf of bread costing three lei in in 1990 and 500 lei six years later.
A group of influential technocrats, in a study issued at the weekend, suggested that Romania's reforms were out of step with its neighbours and that it was time for change.

"Instead of a modern, free and developed society, we are building a society of survival with a democracy of window-dressing and a backward and vulnerable economy," said the study drawn up by the Foundation for a Future for Romania.
